title: Apparitions and private revelation (CCC 67)
hookLine: no apparition is required belief, even approved ones

lines: PLACES WHERE PEOPLE SAY MARY APPEARED.
cards: A woman at a parish fish fry says, between bites, that she's never been sure about Lourdes. The man across from her nearly drops his fork. Doesn't the Church approve it?

Isn't that part of being Catholic? The next days make it urgent: a grotto in France, a field in Portugal, a church wall in Ireland, a school in Rwanda, a forest in Vietnam, all places where people say Mary appeared.
First, the rule the Church uses for all of them. It's short, it's in the Catechism, and it may surprise the man with the fork.

teach.h: IN CHRIST, GOD HAS SAID EVERYTHING.
teach.b: Begin with public revelation. The Letter to the Hebrews says God spoke in many ways through the prophets, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "last of all, in these days hath spoken to us by his Son."
The Catechism draws the conclusion: in Christ, God has said everything, and no new public revelation is to be expected before Christ comes again. That's the faith the whole Church holds and hands on.

Then paragraph sixty-seven, and the other kind. Over the centuries, it says, there have been so-called private revelations, some recognized by the Church's authority. Private doesn't mean secret; a crowd might see it.

teach.h: PRIVATE: OUTSIDE THE DEPOSIT OF FAITH.
teach.b: It means they don't belong to the deposit of faith. Their job isn't to improve or complete Christ's revelation, but to help people live by it more fully in a particular time.

Next, what approval means. When the Church approves a reported apparition, it's saying, in effect: nothing here contradicts the faith, and you may honor it. It isn't saying every Catholic is bound to believe it happened.
The woman at the fish fry is free to stay unsure. The man is free to make a pilgrimage. Neither is a better Catholic for it.
Paul gives one to an early church: "Despise not prophecies. But prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

teach.h: PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.
teach.b: Not scorn, and not swallowing everything: testing, and keeping what's good.

how: The Catholic Church distinguishes public revelation, completed in Christ, from private revelations such as approved apparitions; Catholics may honor approved apparitions and visit their shrines, but are not required to believe in them.

o: a vision kept secret and shown only to a few
a personal sense of God calling you to a vocation
a vision that may help faith but never adds to it

p: hold fast that which is good

s: private revelation means a secret message
private means it isn't part of the deposit of faith. a crowd might see it.
the Catechism says private revelations don't complete Christ's revelation
CCC 67: their role is to help people live it more fully in a particular time.
once the Church approves an apparition, Catholics must believe it
approval means nothing in it contradicts the faith and it may be honored. no one is required to believe it.

games.q: a parishioner tells you she has never been sure about an apparition the Church approved. what does Catholic teaching say about her?
o: she's out of step and should accept it.
she must keep quiet about her doubts.
games.why: no apparition is required belief, even an approved one. private revelations are outside the deposit of faith; approval permits honoring them, it doesn't oblige.

practice: Bring to mind a story you've heard of a vision, a healing or a sign, and notice which way you lean: toward it, wanting it true, or away, ready to roll your eyes.

Neither lean is wrong; just notice it, and hold the story the way you'd hold something fragile that belongs to someone else, open hand, no squeezing. If you pray, ask for the grace to keep what's good.

wordCard.voice: Private revelation. A vision or message, even a public one, that isn't part of the faith the whole Church must believe. It can help people live the Gospel; it can never add to it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: revelation, the word that names the last book of the Bible, which the Douay-Rheims calls the Apocalypse.

carryVoice: Your line: never required. Approved means permitted, not required. Back tomorrow, same hill.
